query: A Wedding Upstairs {A miller's daughter from the next valley married this afternoon, and the party has moved upstairs at the Newt to keep going.|Another wedding upstairs: a carter and a dressmaker, and both families determined to out-dance the other.|A wedding again, and the fiddler from last time, who waves at you with his bow.} The landlady wants the dancing kept going and the families kept apart. Keep everyone dancing {You dance with every aunt, two uncles and the bride. By midnight the families are singing the same song. Both fathers tip you.|You get the two grandmothers dancing together, and after that nobody can remember the feud. The tips are enormous; your feet are not.|The fiddler and you keep it going until the candles go out. You walk home with a pocket of coins and a flower in your hair.} {You ask the wrong cousin to dance, and the families end up on opposite sides of the room. A thin tip, and a long night.|The groom's brother picks a fight with the bride's, and you're the one standing between them. The landlady pays you off early.|Nobody wants to dance with the hired help tonight. You stand by the wall for four hours.} Mind the food and the fire {You keep the platters full and the fire fed. Nobody notices you, which at a wedding is a kind of success.|You carry cake until your arms ache. The bride kisses your cheek on her way out, and you go home sticky and paid.|You mind the fire and watch the dancing. It's honest money, and the music is good.}
